title: Constraints on the Origin of Universal $1/f^2$ Photon-Count Spectra at Baseband
authors: Malvin Carl Teich, Steven B. Lowen
abstract: A series of 11.6-d-duration photon-counting experiments, employing a broad variety of light sources with different statistical properties and optical spectra, were carried out over a 1.5-yr period. All of the photon-count spectra at baseband followed a common $1/f^2$ form over the frequency range $1 \times 10^{-6} \leqslant f \leqslant 5 \times 10^{-4}$ Hz, corresponding to a timescale range $33$ min $ \leqslant T_f \leqslant 11.6$ d, where $T_f \equiv 1/f$. The lower and upper timescale limits were established by the photodetector noise floor and the duration of the individual experiments, respectively. Unlike ordinary Brownian motion, all of the measured photon-count sample paths exhibited irregular long-timescale fluctuations, with durations ranging from hours to days. It has been established that the photon-count spectra cannot plausibly be ascribed to fluctuations of the current, voltage, or temperature of the source or the detector, nor to technical sources of noise associated with the optical system or local environment. Although the physical origin of the photon-count fluctuations remains unresolved, several heterodox hypotheses are set forth. From a statistical point-of-view, the photon counts appear to follow a doubly stochastic Poisson process with a slowly varying random intensity. Analogous experiments that rely on ionizing radiation and direct-conversion solid-state radiation detectors are proposed.
summary: This paper reports extensive experiments showing that photon counts from various light sources exhibit a universal $1/f^2$ spectral signature at low frequencies. After ruling out instrumental and source-specific noise, the authors propose that the fluctuations follow a doubly stochastic Poisson process, suggesting a fundamental physical mechanism beyond simple classical noise sources.
main_problem: The paper investigates the universal origin of a $1/f^2$ spectral signature observed in photon-count fluctuations at baseband across diverse optical sources.
main_result: The observed $1/f^2$ spectrum is robust across different sources and cannot be explained by standard technical noise or source/detector fluctuations. The underlying process is statistically modeled as a doubly stochastic Poisson process.
method: The authors performed long-term photon-counting experiments, analyzing the resulting periodograms and scalograms to characterize the low-frequency spectral density.
model_or_system: The experiments utilized five classes of light sources (LEDs, SLEDs, LDs, incandescent, betaluminescent) and employed photon-counting detectors over periods up to 11.6 days. The analysis compares these measurements against theoretical models like Brownian motion and gravitational wave backgrounds.
key_observables: Photon-count spectra exhibiting a consistent $1/f^2$ form over the frequency range $1 	imes 10^{-6} \le f \le 5 	imes 10^{-4}$ Hz.
important_parameters: Timescale range $33$ min $\le T_f \le 11.6$ d; spectral slope of $f^{-2}$; comparison to GWB spectral slopes ($f^{-7/3}$).
main_assumptions: The fluctuations are assumed to follow a doubly stochastic Poisson process with a slowly varying random intensity, and the analysis compares the results against standard models like GWB.
figures_summary: Figures display averaged periodograms and scalograms showing the characteristic $1/f^2$ or $T^2$ decay for various sources, and compare these to source current/voltage periodograms.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the empirical observation of the $1/f^2$ spectrum across multiple sources, rules out common noise sources, statistically characterizes the process, and finally compares the spectral signature to astrophysical models like the Gravitational Wave Background.
why_interesting: The robust, universal nature of the $1/f^2$ noise, independent of the light source physics, suggests a fundamental, non-trivial underlying physical process that could relate to complex stochastic processes in quantum optics or condensed matter noise sources.
